stem: A freshwater bony fish lives in water that is hypotonic to its body fluids. To osmoregulate it
options: drinks large amounts of water and excretes salt through its gills
produces very little, highly concentrated urine
stores urea in its blood to raise its osmotic pressure
excretes large volumes of dilute urine
explanation: Water keeps entering the fish by osmosis, so its kidneys remove the excess as plenty of dilute urine, while the gills actively take up salts. Drinking water and excreting salt is what a marine bony fish does, and storing urea is the shark's method.

stem: A marine bony fish loses water by osmosis to the sea. It makes up for this by
options: drinking sea water and excreting excess salt through its gills
absorbing large amounts of water through its skin from the sea around it
producing large volumes of dilute urine
storing extra urea in its blood
explanation: Sea water is hypertonic to its body fluids, so the fish drinks it and chloride cells in the gills actively remove the extra salt; it makes only a little urine. Producing large volumes of dilute urine would make the water loss worse.

stem: In humans, the main nitrogenous waste is urea, which is made in the
options: kidneys
liver
urinary bladder
small intestine
explanation: Liver cells convert toxic ammonia from excess amino acids into urea through the ornithine cycle. The kidneys only filter urea out of the blood and the bladder stores the urine.

stem: Birds, reptiles and insects excrete mainly uric acid because it
options: is the most toxic nitrogenous waste
dissolves easily in large amounts of water
needs very little water for its removal
is the cheapest waste to make in terms of energy and requires no enzymes
explanation: Uric acid is nearly insoluble and of low toxicity, so it can be excreted as a paste with very little water, which also suits development inside a shelled egg. Ammonia is the most toxic and needs the most water, which is why mainly aquatic animals excrete it.

stem: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the
options: neuron
alveolus
glomerulus alone
nephron
explanation: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, each with a glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, tubules and loop of Henle that together form urine. The glomerulus is only the capillary knot at the start of a nephron.

stem: In the nephron, ultrafiltration of blood takes place from the
options: loop of Henle into the medulla
collecting duct into the pelvis
glomerulus into Bowman's capsule
distal tubule into the capillaries
explanation: High blood pressure in the glomerulus, because its outgoing arteriole is narrower than the incoming one, forces water and small solutes into Bowman's capsule. Large proteins and blood cells stay behind; the other regions handle reabsorption and secretion.

stem: In a healthy person, almost all the glucose in the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed in the
options: proximal convoluted tubule
loop of Henle
collecting duct
Bowman's capsule, before reaching the tubule
explanation: Cells of the proximal convoluted tubule have microvilli and many mitochondria and actively reabsorb all glucose and amino acids. Glucose appears in the urine only when the blood level is so high that these carriers are saturated, as in untreated diabetes.

stem: When a person is dehydrated, the urine becomes small in volume and concentrated because
options: less ADH is secreted, making the collecting ducts impermeable to water
more ADH is secreted, making collecting ducts more permeable to water
aldosterone stops all salt reabsorption
the glomerulus stops filtering blood
explanation: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect concentrated blood and the posterior pituitary releases more ADH; the collecting ducts then let more water pass back into the salty medulla. Less ADH would produce a large volume of dilute urine.

stem: Desert mammals such as the kangaroo rat can produce very concentrated urine mainly because they have
options: no glomeruli and so no filtration
very long loops of Henle that build a high salt concentration in the medulla
collecting ducts that cannot be affected by ADH
sweat glands that remove urea
explanation: The longer the loop of Henle, the steeper the salt gradient that the countercurrent mechanism creates in the medulla, so more water can be drawn out of the collecting ducts. Collecting ducts that ignore ADH would produce dilute urine instead.

stem: On a hot day in Karachi, the skin helps lose heat from the body mainly by
options: narrowing of skin arterioles and shivering
raising the body hairs and trapping a warm layer of air
increasing the metabolic rate of the liver
widening of skin arterioles and secretion of sweat
explanation: Vasodilation brings more warm blood near the surface to lose heat, and evaporation of sweat removes latent heat. Vasoconstriction, shivering and raised hairs are responses to cold.

stem: The temperature-regulating centre (thermostat) of the human body is located in the
options: cerebellum
medulla oblongata
hypothalamus
thyroid gland
explanation: The hypothalamus monitors blood temperature and starts responses such as sweating or shivering. The thyroid raises metabolic rate under its control, but does not sense temperature.

stem: The hip and shoulder joints, which allow movement in many directions, are
options: ball-and-socket joints
hinge joints
pivot joints
fixed (fibrous) joints
explanation: The rounded head of one bone fits into a cup of another, allowing rotation and movement in all planes. Hinge joints such as the elbow and knee move in one plane only.

stem: According to the sliding filament theory, when a skeletal muscle fibre contracts,
options: the I-band and H-zone shorten while the A-band stays the same length
the A-band shortens while the I-band stays the same
both the actin and the myosin filaments themselves become much shorter
the Z-lines move further apart from each other
explanation: Actin filaments slide over myosin towards the centre of the sarcomere, so the Z-lines come closer and the regions containing only actin (I-band) or only myosin (H-zone) shrink. The A-band equals the length of the myosin filaments, which do not change.

stem: In skeletal muscle, contraction is triggered when calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
options: bind to myosin heads and break ATP
join actin filaments to Z-lines
close the channels in the sarcolemma
bind to troponin, uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin
explanation: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin away from the binding sites on actin; myosin heads can then attach, form cross-bridges and pull. ATP is split by the myosin head itself, not by calcium.

stem: In plants, sclerenchyma gives mechanical support because its cells
options: are living cells with thin cellulose walls
have thick lignified walls and are usually dead at maturity
are living cells that are thickened only at their corners with pectin
stay turgid by filling with water
explanation: Fibres and sclereids have heavily lignified secondary walls, giving strength even after the cell contents die. Living cells thickened at the corners describe collenchyma, and support by turgor is typical of parenchyma.
